title: Omeprazole for babies born early or full-term, who are experiencing reflux
official: Omeprazole for Treatment of Term and preterm infants with gastro-oEsophageal Reflux (OTTER)
summary:
Background and study aims
Gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) is when milk and acid come back up from the stomach after feeds. Mild symptoms of reflux, such as crying or being sick, are experienced by most babies, and often get better over a few months. In some babies, symptoms can be severe with pain, excessive crying and poor weight gain. Parents/caregivers find these symptoms distressing and ask for help from their doctor or health visitor, who may refer them onto specialist paediatricians. Simple things like keeping the baby upright during and after feeds or products that thicken milk can be useful. For severe symptoms, health professionals often use medicines such as omeprazole, that reduce stomach acid. Omeprazole is widely used, but it is not clear if it is effective, and some studies have suggested long-term effects like infections and broken bones. 

Who can participate?
Term and preterm infants with gastro-oesophageal reflux.

What does the study involve?
We want to test omeprazole to find out if it is effective and safe in the long term. We will explain the study to parents/caregivers attending participating GP practices or hospitals with concerns about GOR in their baby. If they consent for their baby to participate, they will be prescribed omeprazole or a ‘placebo’ that looks and tastes like omeprazole but doesn’t contain any active medicine. The treatment will be selected at random by a computer, with babies having a 50/50 chance of receiving either treatment. Parents/caregivers and healthcare professionals will not know which treatment the baby will have. Treatment will be given for 4 weeks, followed by an online questionnaire about their baby’s symptoms. Follow up will continue for 6 months to look for longer-term effects of omeprazole and GOR on growth, infections, fractures and quality of life for parents/carers. Parents will be contacted regularly throughout this period to collect information on outcomes. We will also talk to parents and health professionals in-depth about their experiences of being in the study. The findings will help change practice and inform national guidelines.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Benefits:
Not provided at time of registration
Risks:
One of the concerns for infants taking drugs such as omeprazole that lower stomach acidity, is that longer term use can increase the risk of infections, and fractures. Omeprazole is widely used for treating infants with GOR, and as such the risk of the research is no greater than the risk with infants taking omeprazole as per standard care. However, this may cause concern for the parents/caregivers, and trial materials have been developed to ensure they are aware of that risk, and the limitation in our knowledge of the risks from current research evidence. Parents/caregivers of infants with GOR often find the condition very distressing. To help provide support throughout the trial we have ensured that regular contact will be made in the form of a 2 week well-being phone call, and contact from the trial team during the longer follow up period to 6 months. Trial materials have made it clear that the care and well-being of the infant always comes first.
Parents/caregivers of babies in the trial and their clinicians will be blinded to the treatment allocation. If at any point during the trial, knowledge of the baby's treatment allocation becomes essential for clinical management in an emergency situation, emergency unblinding will be performed in the trial database by site staff who have been delegated the responsibility. The baby's clinical care team will then be able to decide whether to continue the trial treatment. If a SUSAR were to occur, emergency unblinding will take place as necessary to ensure the medical oversight of the CI and/or deputy medical monitor.
In order to minimise the burden of data collection by questionnaire we will be sending links to parents/caregivers by text or email so they can directly access the database on phone or computer. This will make outcome collection adaptable to the needs of different individuals. By providing a paper questionnaire where necessary we will avoid data poverty being an excluding factor to potential participants.

Where is the study run from?
University of Nottingham (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
July 2026 to August 2028.

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK). 

Who is the main contact?
OTTER@nottingham.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Population 1 (Preterm infants):
1.	Infants born <37 weeks’ gestation who are over 32 weeks corrected gestational age (8 weeks before their due date) and under 6 months past their due date at time of trial entry
2.	Must be on full milk feeds at the time of eligibility assessment
3.	Clinical diagnosis of symptomatic GOR made by a suitably qualified healthcare professional following clinical assessment
4.	NICE guideline first-line interventions (including, but not limited to, feed thickeners and alginates) have either already been tried, or considered and are felt to be inappropriate by the treating clinician

Population 2 (Term-born Infants):
1.	Infants born ≥37 weeks’ gestation and who are under 6 months of age
2.	Clinical diagnosis of symptomatic GOR made by a suitably qualified healthcare professional following clinical assessment
3.	NICE guideline first-line interventions (including, but not limited to, feed thickeners and alginates) have either already been tried, or considered and are felt to be inappropriate by the treating clinician
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Surgical conditions affecting feeding or the gastrointestinal tract, including but not limited to repaired oesophageal or intestinal atresia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia and gastroschisis/exomphalos 
2.	Progressive or severe neurological conditions affecting feeding
3.	Infant has received any omeprazole or other proton-pump inhibitors in the preceding 2 weeks
4.	Infant has known hypersensitivity to omeprazole or any of its excipients
5.	Previous participation in the OTTER trial
